\title{HARE: High-Throughput Authenticated Encryption\\
for RISC-V GPGPUs via an ISE}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Anonymous authors}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Paper under double-blind review}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Authenticated encryption is entering the critical data path of confidential
accelerators. Software AEAD preserves programmability but consumes SIMT
resources; fixed-function engines instead dedicate area and create a separate
state-management domain. We implement complete AES-GCM and
ChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing paths at four comparison points in the open-source
Vortex RISC-V GPGPU: S0 software, S1 lane-local primitives, S2 persistent
stateful engines, and S3 subgroup-cooperative instructions. From this study we
derive HARE, an S3 ISE that uses fixed routing so an aligned subgroup can
collectively advance register-resident state.

HARE maps AES and GHASH to four lanes and the ChaCha state to sixteen;
Poly1305 reuses the same SG16 record mapping. Live state remains architectural
between instructions, and no unit-private cryptographic state remains
architecturally live after retirement. We deploy both HARE paths in a Combined
evaluation image that retains the S1 forms used for same-image anchors.
Gated DE10-Pro measurements show large-footprint marginal-cost reductions of
\AESBoardSpeedup{} and \ChaChaBoardSpeedup{} over those lane-local baselines.
The comparison exposes an intercept--slope tradeoff: persistent engines can
amortize short-record setup, whereas HARE avoids persistent unit-private
context. Place-and-route shows that ChaCha SG16 adds 3.4\% ALMs over S1, while
Combined HARE, with one GHASH multiplier array shared across its quads,
remains 58{,}396 ALMs smaller than the standalone ChaCha engine.
% TODO(u5c): 3.4% and 58,396 re-sync once sg16 and chacha-s2p re-fit.
The results show that state lifetime, lane scope, and operation granularity
must be co-designed for programmable SIMT authenticated encryption.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Confidential GPU computing extends trusted execution into the accelerator,
but sensitive data, model state, and intermediate results still cross
CPU--GPU and GPU--GPU links outside the package trust boundary. Those
transfers require confidentiality and integrity
~\cite{nvidia-h100-cc,wang2024fastrack,lee2025gputee}. When authenticated
encryption cannot sustain link rate, cryptographic processing---rather than
the interconnect alone---limits protected throughput.

Software AEAD preserves algorithm agility and composes with GPU kernels, but
competes with the application for issue bandwidth, registers, and lanes. A
fixed-function engine removes work from the SIMT pipeline at the cost of
dedicated area and a separate state-management domain. CPU cryptographic ISA
extensions occupy a useful middle ground
~\cite{gueron2010aesni,riscv-scalar-crypto,riscv-vector-crypto}, yet existing
CPU extensions do not answer three SIMT-specific questions: whether state
survives instruction retirement, how many lanes one instruction may read, and
how much work one invocation completes.

These choices interact with algorithm structure. AES-GCM operates on a
128-bit AES round state and a 128-bit GHASH accumulator; on an RV32 SIMT
machine, each maps directly to four 32-bit lane registers
~\cite{sp800-38d,mcgrew2004gcm}. ChaCha20 instead transforms a 512-bit state
comprising sixteen 32-bit words~\cite{rfc8439,bernstein2008chacha}, whereas
Poly1305 updates an accumulator modulo $2^{130}-5$
~\cite{rfc8439,bernstein2005poly}. Ratified RV32 AES instructions allow
secret-indexed table accesses to be replaced by register-based round
operations~\cite{riscv-scalar-crypto}. ChaCha20's add--xor--rotate steps, by
contrast, already map directly to integer and bit-manipulation datapaths. Its
larger SIMT opportunity is therefore to retain all sixteen words across a
subgroup and advance the fixed column--diagonal dataflow at double-round
granularity.

To study these choices systematically, we implement both sealing paths at
four points in the RTL of the open-source Vortex GPGPU
~\cite{tine2021vortex}: S0 software, S1 lane-local primitives, S2 engines with
persistent per-(warp,\,lane) context, and S3 subgroup-cooperative operations.
This ladder identifies S3 as HARE's selected structure; S0--S2 serve as
comparators. HARE denotes the selected S3 subgroup instructions. Its live
block state remains in ordinary architectural registers across instructions;
a multi-cycle operation may hold transient working values, but no
unit-private cryptographic state remains architecturally live after
retirement. Complete kernels use the existing scalar ISA for setup and
boundary handling. The Combined evaluation image instantiates SG4 for
AES/GHASH and SG16 for the ChaCha state, folds Poly1305 into the same record
mapping, and retains the S1 vocabulary used for same-image anchors.

On the DE10-Pro prototype, HARE reduces large-footprint marginal cost over
same-image S1 anchors by \AESBoardSpeedup{} for AES-GCM and
\ChaChaBoardSpeedup{} for ChaCha20-Poly1305. S2 and HARE optimize different
regimes: S2 amortizes short-record setup through persistent context, whereas
HARE avoids that context and targets lower long-stream marginal cost. Post-fit
results show that ChaCha SG16 adds only 3.4\% ALMs over S1 and that the Combined
HARE build is smaller than the standalone ChaCha S2 engine.

This paper makes three contributions:
\begin{itemize}
\item an implemented S0--S3 comparison of complete AES-GCM and
  ChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing paths on an open-source RISC-V GPGPU;
\item HARE, a subgroup-cooperative ISE that matches lane scope and operation
  granularity to each AEAD while keeping inter-instruction working state in
  architectural registers;
\item on-board evaluation of the intercept--slope and state-lifetime tradeoff,
  together with a timing-closed Combined FPGA implementation of both HARE
  paths.
\end{itemize}

\section{Background}\label{sec:background}

\subsection{SIMT execution and record mapping}
A SIMT core executes \emph{warps} of $W$ logical lanes. A warp issues one
instruction under an active mask, while each lane has private architectural
register state; divergence may deactivate lanes. We call $g$ consecutive,
aligned lanes a \emph{subgroup}. HARE's SG4 and SG16 operations require all
participating lanes to be active and converged. In the evaluated $W{=}16$
Vortex configuration~\cite{tine2021vortex}, lane-local kernels map one
independent record to each lane, SG4 maps one record to each four-lane
subgroup, and SG16 maps one record to the whole warp. Wider cooperation thus
trades record-level concurrency for making more of one record available to a
single instruction; whether that trade pays is an empirical question.

\subsection{AEAD dataflow and state lifetimes}
Authenticated-encryption sealing maps a key $K$, nonce $N$, associated data
(AAD) $A$, and plaintext $P$ to ciphertext $C$ and a tag $T$. AES-128-GCM combines
counter-mode encryption with GHASH~\cite{sp800-38d,mcgrew2004gcm}. Each
16-byte payload block is encrypted as
$C_i=P_i\oplus\mathrm{AES}_{K}(\mathrm{ctr}_i)$, while authentication updates
$Y_i=(Y_{i-1}\oplus X_i)H$ in $\mathrm{GF}(2^{128})$, with
$H=\mathrm{AES}_K(0^{128})$ and $Y_0=0$; $X_i$ covers padded AAD, ciphertext,
and a final length block. The $\mathrm{ctr}_i$ values are successive counters
derived from GCM's pre-counter block $J_0$. Once counters are assigned, AES
blocks are independent, whereas GHASH is defined by an ordered accumulator
recurrence whose terms may be algebraically grouped. AES-128 uses ten rounds.
Its round state, GHASH accumulator $Y$, and subkey $H$ are each 128 bits,
represented as four RV32 words. Under one key, $K$ and $H$ may be reused
across records; $N$, $J_0$, and $Y$ are per-record; the counter and AES
working state are per-block.

ChaCha20-Poly1305 constructs a 512-bit ChaCha state from eight key words,
three nonce words, constants, and a counter
~\cite{rfc8439,bernstein2008chacha,bernstein2005poly}. Let
$Z_i=\mathrm{ChaCha20Block}_K(N,i)$. Ten double rounds, each containing four
column and four diagonal quarter rounds, generate one 64-byte $Z_i$. Counter
zero derives the one-time Poly1305 key; payload encryption starts at counter
one. Poly1305 authenticates AAD, ciphertext, padding, and lengths through an
accumulator recurrence, represented in our implementation by five 26-bit
limbs. The ChaCha key may be reused, whereas the nonce, Poly1305 key, and
accumulator are per-record; the counter and working state are per-block. Both
AEADs require a unique nonce for every record under a fixed key. Accelerating
ChaCha alone therefore does not complete the AEAD path.
Figure~\ref{fig:aead-flow} makes the common asymmetry between independent
cipher blocks and authentication recurrences explicit.

\subsection{From algorithm structure to design choices}
State width suggests a subgroup scope, but does not determine a complete
instruction. Poly1305 illustrates the distinction: its five-limb accumulator
does not itself imply SG16. HARE uses SG16 because the ChaCha20-Poly1305 kernel
already maps one record to the sixteen lanes holding the ChaCha state, and one
64-byte ciphertext block supplies four consecutive 16-byte Poly1305 blocks.
The instruction can therefore absorb those four blocks while preserving one
record mapping across cipher and authenticator. More generally, state
lifetime, lane scope, and work per invocation are independent architectural
choices. Section~\ref{sec:space} organizes the implemented alternatives into
the S0--S3 comparison ladder.

\section{The design space: where the state lives}\label{sec:space}

We organize AEAD ISEs for SIMT machines into four tiers along three
architectural choices: where live cryptographic state resides and whether it
persists beyond retirement, how many lanes one instruction may read, and how
much cryptographic work one invocation performs (Fig.~\ref{fig:tiers}).

\textbf{S0 --- software.} State lives in per-lane registers and memory; an
instruction reads two registers of one lane. Every state move and table
lookup is explicit.

\textbf{S1 --- lane-local.} State remains in per-lane registers. Each
instruction performs one cipher step but sees operands only from its own
lane. The AES-GCM instance uses the ratified scalar-cryptography vocabulary;
the ChaCha20-Poly1305 instance uses custom scalar fusions because no ratified
ChaCha- or Poly1305-specific instructions exist.

\textbf{S2 --- stateful engine.} State moves into persistent unit-private
context addressed by (warp,\,lane). Its fields have different lifetimes:
the ChaCha key and GHASH subkey $H$ may persist across records; the nonce and
GHASH accumulator are initialized per record; AES working state and its
initial round key are installed per block because the on-the-fly schedule
mutates the stored key; and \texttt{chacha.begin} supplies a per-block
counter. The smaller instruction stream therefore comes with storage for
every (warp,\,lane) and an explicit ownership, validity, and zeroization
contract.

\textbf{S3 --- subgroup-cooperative.} Live state remains in ordinary
architectural registers, distributed one word per lane across an aligned
subgroup. One instruction reads the subgroup's operand vector through
\emph{fixed} lane routing (no crossbar), writes one result per lane, and may
hold transient working values while in flight; no unit-private state remains
valid after retirement. S2 changes state lifetime and location, whereas S3
changes which lanes an instruction may read.

Three properties frame everything that follows. S1--S3 instructions have
fixed, operand-independent latency, and the measured sealing kernels do not
derive addresses from keys or plaintext. This is narrower than a complete
side-channel-resistance claim: shared-resource contention, power/EM leakage,
and physical residue are outside our evaluation. Subgroup instructions
require a fully converged group. SimX aborts and RTL simulation asserts when
only part of an SG4 or SG16 group is active; synthesized hardware assumes
software maintains this invariant. S1 and S3 add no unit-private state beyond
retirement, but their architectural registers still rely on the GPU's normal
save, restore, and clearing rules. Only S2 adds a persistent unit-private key
namespace.

\section{Instruction-set implementations}\label{sec:ise}

Table~\ref{tab:isa} lists the hardware instructions evaluated across S1--S3.
HARE comprises the selected S3 forms. The Combined evaluation image also
retains the S1 vocabulary used for same-image anchors; S2 engine instructions
are comparison-only. Three format facts frame the table. The
only three-source instruction \emph{family} is the S1
Poly1305 multiply-accumulate family, which is R4-type and reuses the operand
path already present for gather---no read port is added. Every subgroup
instruction fits the existing two-read/one-write delivery path; several are
2R1W, while \texttt{chacha.dr.sg16} is 1R1W. The engines' streaming
operations write \texttt{x0}, so they produce no
scoreboard entry at all: ordering comes from the unit itself, which stalls
issue while busy.

\subsection{S1: lane-local scalar primitives}
The measured AES-GCM S1 path uses five ratified instruction forms:
\texttt{aes32esi}/\texttt{aes32esmi} (Zkne) compute one byte's
round step, and \texttt{clmul}/\texttt{clmulh} (Zbkc) with \texttt{brev8}
(Zbkb) build GHASH in the reflected domain, the accumulator and hash subkey
living in ordinary registers. Because these are existing ratified per-lane
forms, we treat S1 rather than S0 as the novelty baseline; their measured
benefit is specific to the evaluated Vortex configuration.

RISC-V defines no ratified ChaCha20- or Poly1305-specific instructions, so the
corresponding S1 path adds two custom forms. \texttt{chacha32.xr} fuses the XOR and left-rotate that end
every ARX line, turning a three-instruction line into two---and buys almost
nothing ($1.09\times$ alone), because the line's add remains and the round
count is untouched. \texttt{poly26.mac} is the instruction that matters: a
26-bit limb multiply-accumulate whose low/high split is exact rather than
approximate (the low form accumulates products mod $2^{26}$, the high form
their quotients), R4-type on the machine's existing three-source path.

\subsection{S2: stateful engines}
Context-write instructions (\texttt{.cwr}) load key material into
unit-private storage addressed by (warp,\,lane); streaming instructions then
advance whole rounds or blocks against it. Three folds keep the streams
short. The AES engine runs its key schedule \emph{on the fly}
(\texttt{aes.rndm} computes $\mathrm{NextKey}$ as it rounds, so no expanded
schedule is ever stored or loaded); \texttt{ghash.cwr} XORs the incoming
block into the accumulator as it writes, absorbing for free; and
\texttt{chacha.begin} rebuilds the whole 512-bit initial state from one
counter operand, so after the key has been installed and the per-record nonce
has been written, \emph{a ChaCha block costs no context writes at all};
\texttt{chacha.crd} folds the
feed-forward add into the read. The ChaCha context is 896 bits per
(warp,\,lane)---512 state, 256 key, 96 nonce, 32 counter---which at four
warps and sixteen lanes is 57{,}344 bits per core. Context is per lane, not
per warp, by design: sharing one key per warp was rejected because batching
records from \emph{different} sessions---different keys in the same
warp---is the case that makes a GPU worth using for AEAD at all.
There is deliberately no Poly1305 engine: five limbs live in ten registers
and a block step is ten three-source MACs, so the ChaCha-Poly S2 row pairs
its cipher engine with the lane-local \texttt{poly26.mac}; GHASH's full
GF($2^{128}$) block step is where a stateful authenticator pays, which is
why only the AES-GCM S2 row is a dual engine.

\subsection{HARE: S3 subgroup-cooperative instructions}
For AES-GCM the subgroup is an aligned quad: lane $i$ holds column $i$ of
the 128-bit state, \texttt{aesrm.sg4}/\texttt{aesrf.sg4} perform a complete
round each (the ShiftRows lane exchange is fixed wiring), and
\texttt{ghmul.sg4} a full GF($2^{128}$) multiply, at the price of four
carry-less multipliers per lane where the lane-local path needs one---the
area consequence appears in Table~\ref{tab:area}.

At sixteen lanes, lane $i$ holds word $i$ and \texttt{chacha.dr.sg16}
advances one full double round per instruction---ten per block. It executes
as a fixed ten-cycle sequence over the 512-bit ChaCha state, owner-locked
while in flight; no unit-private value remains valid after retirement.
\texttt{poly4.step.sg16} absorbs a whole 64-byte ChaCha block---four
Poly1305 blocks---in one instruction: the accumulator $h$ travels in lanes
0--4, the key $r$ in lanes 5--9 of the \emph{same} source register, and the
result returns $h'$ with $r$ untouched, so the output feeds the next absorb
directly. The $r^2,r^3,r^4$ schedule that block-parallel software Poly1305
must hold in registers (we measure it at 20 loads per block and 36\% of
kernel cycles) exists only inside the unit, and never becomes architectural.
The Poly1305 macro contains approximately 642 additional transient bits; the
complete double-round/Poly1305 pair therefore holds about 1{,}154
instruction-local working bits in total, not 1{,}154 bits in
\texttt{chacha.dr.sg16} itself.
The line-granular SG16 control is confined to Sec.~\ref{sec:eval} and does not
belong to the deployable HARE configuration.

\subsection{Encoding}
Packing $h$ and $r$ into one operand is what keeps the sixteen-lane tier
2R1W: the first version of \texttt{poly4.step.sg16} read them from two
registers---five lanes used, eleven dead, in each---and needed an R4-type
third source for the message. Ten of sixteen lanes carry both values with
six to spare; the repack costs +218 ALMs and 17 instructions per message
(under 2\% of cycles), and returns a seven-bit funct7 where R4 offers two
bits. One caution generalizes: our four-bit sub-opcode space filled
completely---all sixteen SYM values are taken, and the sixteen-lane double
round, its stateless ablation, and the S2 engine's round op share one slot,
with the build system refusing any two together---so an extension of this
size should budget opcode space as deliberately as it budgets area.

\section{Methodology}\label{sec:method}

We deploy two Vortex cores, each with four 16-lane warps, on a DE10-Pro
(Stratix~10 1SG280) with one DDR4 channel and a 200\,MHz GPU clock. The
physical board is the final performance source of record. Device cycle and
retired-instruction counters bracket the kernel; PCIe transfer and host launch
are excluded. In the final sweep, each point discards five warm-up launches
and reports the median and interquartile range of 30 runs. Every speedup uses
an S1 anchor from the same FPGA image and software build.

Outputs are checked against NIST GCM- and RFC~8439-derived host references. A
row is admitted only after a normal exit, a reference match, exactly one
\texttt{PERF} record, \texttt{PASSED!}, and a balanced per-core instruction
split. We use 128 records, subject to final on-board saturation confirmation,
and require minimum/maximum per-core retired instructions $\ge 0.99$. The
evaluation covers sealing; opening and tag verification are outside scope.

We fit $C=\alpha+\beta B$ over three power-of-two payload sizes and report
$\beta$ in cycles/byte. Separate small- and large-footprint fits pass an
on-board footprint scan and a 5\% linearity check. Whole-record throughput is
reported when the intercept changes the ordering; diagnostic counters explain
mechanisms but do not supply headline performance.

A board-matched cycle-accurate RTL model is used only as an implementation
cross-check. At two AES-GCM SG4 points, both platforms retire identical
per-core instruction counts and their marginal slopes differ by 0.9\%; no
model-derived cycle count is a final headline result. Area and timing use
Quartus~19.2, a common RTL revision, QSF/SDC constraints, and seed~6. All ten
archived configurations close setup and hold across 30 corner checks.

\noindent\emph{Draft data-source gate.} The numerical performance tables in
this working draft remain provisional development values until the complete
DE10-Pro sweep passes the same gate and regenerates every dependent number;
they are not claimed as board measurements.

\subsection{Different algorithms harvest at different tiers}
Table~\ref{tab:tiers} is the paper's central measurement. Reading the
large-footprint $\times$S1 column: AES-GCM's big step is S0${\to}$S1
(up to $18.2\times$)---the
tier that deletes its table lookups---after which the stateful engine adds
$1.81\times$ and the subgroup form $4.92\times$. ChaCha's S1 buys only
$1.55\times$: ARX was never table-bound, and its costs sit in the sheer
count of round operations, which only round-level instructions (S2/S3)
remove. The design consequence is that a GPGPU that stops at the scalar AES
vocabulary has accelerated AES and left ChaCha largely issue-bound. Stateful
engines reduce marginal cost further and remain valuable for short records,
but they are not the lowest-marginal-cost point and have the largest
incremental area in the measured ladder.
The per-step pattern falls out of Table~\ref{tab:tiers}'s $\times$S1
columns: AES-GCM's largest step is the first, ChaCha's is the second, and
the subgroup step multiplies both at the small-footprint point ($1.49\times$,
$1.61\times$); at the large-footprint point it is decisive for AES-GCM
($2.71\times$) and, for ChaCha, a narrow win ($1.05\times$) whose real
argument is what it does \emph{not} cost---S2's context and its lifetime.
HARE-SG16 achieves the lowest observed marginal cost in both regimes:
essentially tied with S2 in the large-footprint regime (1.728 against
1.807\,\cB) and $1.61\times$ ahead small-footprint, while avoiding
additional persistent unit-private crypto context. That tie is against a
partially engined S2---the row has no Poly1305 engine, and 42\% of its
instructions are the lane-local authenticator---so we measured what an
engine could buy: a diagnostic that deletes every absorb (83\% of the
stream) runs 5\% \emph{slower} (1.890 against 1.807\,\cB). The MACs execute
in the shadow of the engine's eight-cycle double-rounds; an engine's ceiling
is at most zero, and the tie stands.
% Removed 2026-09-03: "without rotate instructions the S0 figure moves only
% 2.4%" came from the superseded n=64 dataset and does not reproduce -- at
% n=128 the plain-software row is 12.5% FASTER per byte than the rori row
% (9.998 vs 11.424 c/B, b=16->32), because rori issues to the SYM unit, not
% the ALU. See data/chacha-s0-rori-20260903.md; the S0 row of record is
% under review.
At both operating points the subgroup tier has the lowest marginal cost for
both AEADs ($5.81\times$ and $8.41\times$ over S1 small-footprint). The first
on-board AES-SG4 cross-check processes 16\,KiB in 36{,}345 cycles and 128\,KiB
in 145{,}492 cycles (0.901\,B/cycle, or 180\,MB/s kernel-only, at the larger
point); its two-point marginal cost is 0.952\,c/B. These validation points are
not substituted for the complete board sweep. Marginal figures cancel per-message
start-up; whole-run throughput at fixed record lengths, which pays it,
appears with the state-placement analysis below, where start-up is
precisely what separates the engine from the macro.

\subsection{Granularity, context, and record size}
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{ChaCha design points at the large footprint; instructions and cycles
are marginal values per 64\,B. Private bits are per in-flight instruction
(ChaCha/Poly for HARE) or per core for S2. The line-granular row is a
non-deployed control.}
\label{tab:state}
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2pt}
\input{tables/tab_state}
\end{table}
The fixed-SG16 comparison cleanly isolates granularity. The stateless
\texttt{chacha.arx.sg16} form advances one ARX line;
the owner-locked \texttt{chacha.dr.sg16} macro holds the 512-bit state for ten
cycles and advances a complete double round. The line-granular form is
$1.78\times$ slower despite using the same subgroup and machine. It needs
$2.88\times$ as many instructions (141 versus 49 per 64-byte block), and
although its IPC rises $1.40\times$ and scoreboard stall falls from 92\% to
76\%, that issue-rate improvement cannot pay for the extra work. Archived
latency ablations are consistent with the same interpretation: doubling warp
count recovered 12\%, and a one-instruction-per-cycle macro pipeline was
1.1\% slower at 13\% unit occupancy because successive operations are
dependent. The controlled result is therefore about granularity: the macro
wins by removing instructions, not by exposing a lower single-cycle latency.

Counters add a memory-system observation for the selected mappings. At
256\,KiB, ChaCha S1-to-SG16 changes DRAM traffic from 78.51 to 49.01\,B/B
and write-hit rate from 1.7\% to 39.1\%; AES S1-to-SG4 changes 48.40 to
9.21\,B/B and 0.1\% to 72.7\%. These changes are consistent with improved
spatial coalescing when unrelated per-lane streams become one record per
natural-width subgroup on the evaluated hierarchy; they do not establish
the same mechanism at every footprint.

The S2 comparison is broader. It changes record mapping and concurrency as
well as state location and lifetime. S2 has the smallest instruction stream
(28.9 instructions per 64-byte block) and large-footprint marginal cost close
to the macro (115.7 versus 110.6 cycles per 64 bytes), but introduces a
persistent per-(warp,\,lane) namespace. Relative to the crypto-free build,
ChaCha S2 adds 112{,}951 ALMs, $2.86\times$ the 39{,}456-ALM increment of
SG16. We implement the engine datapath but not preemption save-or-destroy;
ownership, validity, and zeroize-on-release remain part of its architectural
contract. SG16 keeps live state in ordinary registers and owes only
instruction-local ownership while the macro is in flight.

The slope is only half the trade; per-message start-up is the other half,
and the tiers pay it very differently. Nonce setup, the Poly1305 key
block, and tag finalisation cost the engine about 0.8k cycles per record,
S1 about 1.2k, and the sixteen-lane macro about 8.6k---partly software it
runs sixteen-wide-redundant, partly mapping: one record per subgroup
leaves eight records in flight against S1's 128, so per-record costs
serialise sixteen times deeper. The engine's persistent context is,
mechanically, a device for amortising start-up across a session, and the
macro repays that amortisation with no additional persistent unit-private
state. The affine model places SG16's crossover with S1 near 1.3\,KiB. At
2\,KiB, S2 is $2.9\times$ faster whole-run (0.51 versus 0.18\,B/cycle), and
it remains faster at every measured size through 4\,KiB. Extrapolating the
two fitted lines would put an S2--SG16 crossover near 100\,KiB, well outside
the measured record-size range; we therefore treat it as a design projection,
not an observed result. The measured conclusion is narrower and more useful:
S2 buys short-record amortization with persistent context, whereas SG16 buys
the lower marginal slope without that second state namespace.

One inversion in Table~\ref{tab:tiers} now has its explanation: at S3
\emph{both} algorithms retire more instructions than at S2
($2.7\times$ for AES, $1.7\times$ for ChaCha) and both are faster on the
marginal ($2.71\times$ for AES; $1.05\times$ large-footprint and
$1.61\times$ small-footprint for ChaCha). S2 spends area and lifetime
semantics to shrink the instruction stream; S3 spends issue slots to avoid
additional persistent unit-private context. The appropriate choice therefore
depends on record length and the platform's context-switch contract.

Table~\ref{tab:tiers}'s $\Delta$ALM column prices each tier against the

that area goes and what it took to bring it down.

% ChaCha S1, AES SG4 over AES S1, the S2 engines) re-sync once the
% same-version set completes; do not hand-copy from the current mixed table.
In the first Combined fit one block held two thirds of the extension:
GHASH's GF($2^{128}$) multiply, a schoolbook $4{\times}4$ of 32-bit
carry-less products per four-lane quad, one array per quad---64 multipliers
per core, 62{,}382 ALMs across the two cores against 9{,}538 for the AES
round itself. Two changes to that block, and nothing else, cut it
$2.5\times$. Karatsuba on both levels of the 128-bit product turns sixteen
multiplies into nine, but the deeper XOR combine costs 72\,ps of setup at
200\,MHz. Sharing one nine-multiply array across the four quads---GHASH per
record is a serial chain, so the quads hold independent records and one
array walks them in four cycles---removes three of the four arrays and puts
one quad's Karatsuba, not four in parallel, on the critical path; every
corner closes again. The latency costs nothing measurable: the unit sat at
13\% occupancy on a memory-bound AEAD, and cycles are bit-identical at
16\,KiB and within 0.16\% at 128\,KiB. Combined HARE lands at 238{,}526
ALMs, +54{,}555 (29.7\%) over the crypto-free build and 58{,}396 ALMs
below the standalone ChaCha S2 engines;
% TODO(u5c): 58,396 uses the 09-01 chacha-s2p fit; re-sync after its re-fit.
GHASH is now 45\% of the extension, and what remains of it is the sixteen
lane-local multipliers the S1 tier itself needs plus the one shared array.
Because the extension is a per-lane ISA rather than a shared block, its
cost scales with cores alongside the baseline: the percentage is a
steady-state per-core tax, not one amortised by adding cores.

All ten configurations close setup and hold across the 30 archived corner
checks at common seed~6. The constraint set carries one exclusion---a
single dispatch buffer pinned out of register retiming---which closed the
Combined build's last 2\,ps hold corner; GPU and PCIe timing, RAM/DSP
usage, and the per-corner summaries are retained in the build archive.

Power is read on the board from the two LTC2945 monitors the shell already
carries (12\,V input and the FPGA core rail, about ten samples per second),
sampled inside the measurement process between kernel launches so
telemetry never races the command processor. With the Combined image loaded
and idle the floor is 46.5\,W input and 22.5\,W core, dominated by the PCIe
and DDR4 shell; the quantity of interest is the active-minus-idle delta at
sustained load, from which energy per byte follows with the measured
throughput.
% TODO(power sweep): active deltas and J/B per tier from the gated sweep.

\subsection{Security properties}
All evaluated instruction forms have operand-independent latency, and the
measured sealing
kernels do not derive memory addresses from keys or plaintext; AES S1 also
removes the secret-indexed T-table accesses of S0. This is narrower than a
complete side-channel claim: shared-resource contention, power, EM leakage,
and physical residue are not evaluated. Full-subgroup convergence is a
software precondition. SimX rejects and RTL-simulation assertions detect
partially active SG4 and SG16 groups, while synthesized RTL assumes the
invariant. S1 and S3 retain live secrets in ordinary architectural registers,
which the baseline context-switch policy must save and clear; they add no
unit-private state surviving retirement. S2 additionally retains
per-(warp,\,lane) key context and therefore requires ownership, validity, and
zeroize-on-release rules, which we identify but do not implement.
Instruction-local SG16 working registers may contain sensitive values while
active; HARE does not claim their physical scrubbing at retirement.

\section{Discussion and limitations}\label{sec:discussion}
The S0--S3 study exposes a design rule and a measured tradeoff; HARE selects
S3 without claiming that one tier dominates every deployment. For
ChaCha20-Poly1305, SG16 has the lowest
observed marginal cost and avoids persistent unit-private state, while S2 is
faster for every complete-record size measured through 4\,KiB. Applications
with many short records may rationally choose the engine and pay its context
contract; long streams, kernel composability, and preemptive multi-tenancy make
the subgroup form more attractive. AES-GCM is less ambiguous in our
configuration because SG4 lowers both fitted slopes substantially relative to
S2, but setup still matters to any endpoint-throughput claim.

The counter results explain behavior on the evaluated hierarchy only. Vortex
here has two RV32 cores, sixteen-lane warps, write-through/no-write-allocate
caches, and no L2. The large-footprint coalescing changes are evidence for a
mechanism on that machine, not proof that the same traffic ratios or crossover
will hold with an L2, more cores, a different memory scheduler, or wider warps.
Likewise, AES at SG4 and ChaCha at SG16 instantiate natural-width mappings at
two state sizes; more primitives and machines are needed before treating the
resulting scope-and-granularity guideline as universal.

The board protocol measures kernel-only execution. PCIe transfer and host
launch lie outside this metric, so we do not infer end-to-end application
throughput from a kernel speedup. Place-and-route establishes area and timing
feasibility at a common seed across all reported corner checks, but power and
energy are not yet measured. Finally, Combined HARE implements and validates
sealing but not device-side opening or tag verification, and the exploratory
S2 prototype does not implement preemption save-or-destroy. We do not evaluate
power/EM or contention side channels.

\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}
\textbf{CPU cryptography ISEs.} AES-NI~\cite{gueron2010aesni} and RISC-V's
scalar extensions~\cite{riscv-scalar-crypto,marshall2021aesise} define the
ratified operations used by our AES-GCM S1 baseline. The
ChaCha20-Poly1305 S1 path instead uses custom
lane-local fusions; Marshall et al. study a lightweight scalar ChaCha ISE for
resource-constrained RISC-V cores~\cite{marshall2021chacha}. Our design-space
study asks a different SIMT question: when should work stay lane-local, become
persistent unit context, or span multiple lanes? RISC-V vector
cryptography~\cite{riscv-vector-crypto} already operates on four-element
groups for AES's 128-bit state. HARE instantiates analogous SIMT subgroups at
the natural four- and sixteen-lane extents while making convergence and
per-lane register ownership explicit.

\textbf{Cryptography on Vortex and GPUs.} Adams et al. added a draft RISC-V
cryptography subset to Vortex and accelerated AES and SHA
~\cite{adams2021crypto}; that lane-local execute-unit approach is the closest
antecedent to our S1 baseline and motivates using S1, rather than software, as
the novelty baseline. Our study expands the architectural comparison to persistent and
subgroup-cooperative organizations, implements complete AES-GCM and
ChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing paths, and couples cycle results to same-version
physical fits. GPU software work ranges from CUDA AES
~\cite{manavski2007cuda} to hybrid CPU/GPU ChaCha
~\cite{wang2021gpuchacha} and parallelized GPU GCM/GHASH
~\cite{lee2025gpugcm}. Those systems optimize algorithmic parallelism on
commercial GPU ISAs; HARE instead changes the SIMT ISA and RTL. Our evaluation
uses software as S0 in a controlled tier ladder rather than making
cross-platform throughput comparisons.

\textbf{GPU confidential computing.} Graviton established a GPU-TEE system
design~\cite{volos2018graviton}, and commercial confidential GPUs now protect
execution inside the accelerator package~\cite{nvidia-h100-cc}. Recent work
characterizes distributed-training overheads and reduces protected-I/O
scheduling and overlap costs~\cite{lee2025gputee,wang2024fastrack}. Those
system techniques determine when and where transfers occur; an ISE reduces
the instruction and data-movement cost of the AEAD kernel itself, so the two
approaches compose. Fixed-function link or memory encryptors remain another
valid point: they can deliver high bandwidth, but they do not expose the
algorithm as a programmable SIMT operation and they introduce their own
state, interface, and agility tradeoffs.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
Our S0--S3 study shows that AEAD acceleration on a SIMT machine is a
granularity--concurrency--lifetime tradeoff. Lane-local ratified operations
remove AES-GCM's table bottleneck but custom scalar fusions barely change
ChaCha's long ARX stream. HARE therefore selects subgroup cooperation: four
lanes for AES/GHASH and sixteen lanes with a double-round macro for
ChaCha/Poly1305. Both forms fit the existing register-delivery path and add no
unit-private state that survives retirement.

That choice does not make S3 universally fastest. Persistent S2 context can
reduce fixed cost for short records, but requires the largest incremental area
and a separate ownership and zeroization contract. HARE instead targets lower
marginal cost without that persistent namespace. The deployable Combined HARE build uses
19{,}456 fewer ALMs than standalone ChaCha S2 while containing both
subgroup paths. The broader lesson is to evaluate
an AEAD ISE with both slope and intercept, and to budget state lifetime,
operand delivery, convergence, and opcode space alongside ALMs. Power and
energy, end-to-end transport, more memory hierarchies, and the opening path remain the
next steps.
